name: tuberous sclerosis skin
aliases: cutaneous manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex

clinicalPearls: Cutaneous signs are among the earliest and most useful diagnostic clues to tuberous sclerosis complex and feature prominently in the diagnostic criteria.
Hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules are frequently present from infancy and are best demonstrated under Wood's lamp examination.
Facial angiofibromas develop over the nasolabial folds, cheeks and chin in childhood and are commonly mistaken for acne.
A shagreen patch is a connective-tissue naevus, typically a raised plaque over the lumbosacral region with an orange-peel texture.
Peri- and subungual fibromas (Koenen tumours) tend to appear later, around puberty and adulthood.
A fibrous cephalic (forehead) plaque is a specific skin marker and may precede other features.
The disorder arises from loss-of-function mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 with consequent overactivation of the mTOR pathway.
Topical or systemic mTOR inhibitors can reduce facial angiofibromas and address systemic manifestations under specialist supervision.
reference.pathophysiology: Tuberous sclerosis complex is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in TSC1 (encoding hamartin) or TSC2 (encoding tuberin). The hamartin-tuberin complex normally inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway; its loss releases constitutive mTOR activation, driving unchecked cell growth and the formation of hamartomas across multiple organs. In the skin this dysregulated growth produces the characteristic lesions: hypomelanotic macules reflecting reduced melanogenesis, angiofibromas composed of fibrovascular proliferation, connective-tissue naevi (shagreen patches), and periungual fibromas. The same pathway underlies the systemic hamartomas of brain, kidney, heart and lung, which is why recognition of the skin signs prompts wider evaluation.
additionalDifferentials: Acne vulgaris or rosacea (mimicking facial angiofibromas)
Isolated hypopigmentation such as naevus depigmentosus or vitiligo
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with cutaneous collagenomas
additionalInvestigations: Wood's lamp examination to highlight hypomelanotic macules
Genetic testing for TSC1 and TSC2 mutations
Brain MRI for cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma
Renal imaging for angiomyolipomas and cysts
Echocardiography for cardiac rhabdomyomas, especially in infancy
redFlags: New focal neurological deficit or rising intracranial pressure suggesting subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
Flank pain or haematuria indicating angiomyolipoma haemorrhage
Respiratory symptoms in women suggesting lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Refractory seizures or developmental regression requiring urgent neurological input
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous lesions themselves are benign but can cause considerable cosmetic and psychological burden; overall prognosis is determined by systemic involvement, particularly neurological disease, renal angiomyolipomas and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, and has improved with mTOR-inhibitor therapy and multidisciplinary surveillance.
pitfalls: Treating facial angiofibromas as acne and thereby missing the underlying diagnosis.
Overlooking subtle hypomelanotic macules without Wood's lamp examination.
Assessing skin in isolation and failing to arrange systemic screening once the diagnosis is suspected.
Attributing a solitary skin finding to tuberous sclerosis without applying the full diagnostic criteria.
Neglecting genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant inheritance and variable expressivity.
references: International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Consensus Group diagnostic criteria
management: Topical mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus) applied to facial angiofibromas to reduce their size and vascularity
Ablative or vascular laser therapy, and surgical excision, dermabrasion or curettage for angiofibromas, fibrous cephalic plaques and Koenen tumours
Skin camouflage and psychological support for the cosmetic and social burden of visible lesions
Recognition of the cutaneous signs as a trigger for full multisystem evaluation and systemic mTOR inhibitor therapy where brain, renal or pulmonary disease is present
Periodic dermatological review as lesions such as periungual fibromas emerge and evolve through adolescence and adulthood
Multidisciplinary referral to clinical genetics, neurology and nephrology
Genetic counselling and family screening for autosomal dominant tuberous sclerosis complex
